power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: People with low vision (PLVs) experience difficulties in spatial navigation associated with their low vision (LV) and are inadequately supported by status quo information solutions.
The LV case, in which visual input is present but functionally unreliable, also falls out of scope of existing taxonomies of spatial navigation derived from mostly normally sighted subjects.

We propose three perturbations through which LV adds attentional demands to navigation: we review evidence that it de-automates the task of avoiding obstacles and safely walking (vigilant locomotion), hypothesize that it strains visual search by creating uncertainty about information sources' presence, placement, form, and accessibility (naive search), and conjecture that it lowers confidence for wayfinding decisions, encouraging backtracking and frequent confirmation (fragile decisions).
Empirical evidence supports that vigilant locomotion under LV interferes with concurrent cognitive processes, especially spatial learning.

We hypothesize that this interference extends to wayfinding and that difficulties in information sampling (naive search) and low metacognitive confidence (fragile decisions) additionally strain attention.

Accordingly, we introduce three design aims which can help evaluate whether current and prospective wayfinding information solutions support lowvision navigation by addressing these perturbations; information should be continuous at step-level, easy to sample, and confirmatory via paired feedback.
Future research should directly test these predictions in ecological contexts and investigate the possibility that acute stressors can mimic the LV-related perturbations in the general population.
As my RER B train pulls up  I confirm that, yes, I had taken the correct path.
text.formatted: As my <ref type="bibr">RER B train pulls up</ref>  I confirm that, yes, I had taken the correct path.

text.text: Frustrated and confused, I follow my original path, this time searching more methodically for directions to the 14.
I spot a sign on the wall which points me down another hallway and make my way there to take the moving walkway to a second section of the station.
When I lose my way again, another passenger offers her help, guiding me to a final set of stairs up to the platform.
The train status display reads "14: Saint-Denis -Pleyel," the correct direction.
I have finally reached my platform and can take a seat until the next train arrives.

This trip, an autobiographical snapshot about navigating public transit with low vision (LV), exemplifies three LV-related perturbations to navigation that are key to explaining and intervening in the difficulties people with low vision (PLVs) experience daily while traveling in urban hubs.
PLVs' spatial navigation performance is generally worse than that of people with good vision: they make more errors and take longer to complete navigational tasks (Daga et al., 2017).
text.formatted: PLVs' spatial navigation performance is generally worse than that of people with good vision: they make more errors and take longer to complete navigational tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Daga et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Contrast sensitivity and visual field deficits appear to have a greater negative impact on navigation performance than do visual acuity deficits (Leat & Lovie-Kitchin, 2008; Marron & Bailey, 1982).
text.formatted: Contrast sensitivity and visual field deficits appear to have a greater negative impact on navigation performance than do visual acuity deficits <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Leat & Lovie-Kitchin, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Marron & Bailey, 1982)</ref>.

text.text: PLVs also self-report difficulties in orienting in variable lighting and avoiding peripheral obstacles (Latham et al., 2017).
text.formatted: PLVs also self-report difficulties in orienting in variable lighting and avoiding peripheral obstacles <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Latham et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Poorly located and illegible signs also cause frustration in public transit wayfinding (Boadi-Kusi et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Poorly located and illegible signs also cause frustration in public transit wayfinding <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Boadi-Kusi et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Performance deficits exist for blind people as well, though evidence differs as to whether these deficits are persistent, convergent, or cumulative (see Schinazi et al., 2016, for a review).
text.formatted: Performance deficits exist for blind people as well, though evidence differs as to whether these deficits are persistent, convergent, or cumulative (see <ref type="bibr">Schinazi et al., 2016, for a review)</ref>.

text.text: LV is a uniquely informative case for understanding spatial navigation: it occupies a sui generis cognitive regime wherein visual information is present (in contrast with "total blindness") but is functionally unreliable (in contrast with "normal vision").

We propose that LV reveals the attentional competition of processes which accounts of normally sighted navigation treat as automatic and which accounts of blind navigation describe but to which they do not attribute a cognitive cost.
The narrative provides anecdotal evidence of this attentional competition.

Firstly, the chaotic scene navigating from the platform edge to the escalator exemplifies how ensuring one's safe locomotion and mobility with LV is a demanding process which detracts from one's ability to perform concurrent tasks; we term this vigilant locomotion.

Secondly, the repeated misses of important wayfinding signs illustrate how finding information about one's destination under high uncertainty about this information's existence, form, and accessibility complicates the search task beyond simply locating a target; we term this naive search.

Thirdly, the instance of backtracking to the original source of information about line 14 shows how low confidence can make one prone to seeking confirmatory information and second-guessing one's decisions; we term this fragile decisions.
These three LV-related perturbations co-occurred throughout this single trip, causing confusion, backtracking, and wayfinding failures.
Sections 2.1-2.3 address the three perturbations in turn and detail experiments to empirically test them when applicable, and Section 3 presents the three design aims we derive from them.
>LV-Related Perturbations to Navigation
text.formatted: <head n="2." >LV-Related Perturbations to Navigation</head>

text.text: LV stresses locomotion, which appears to be automatic under normal vision, at the expense of other controlled processes.

Two prominent taxonomies for spatial navigation's constituent processes presuppose locomotion and sign detection and explicitly place these processes outside their scope. Montello (2005) and Wiener and colleagues (2009) emphasize the distinction between locomotion (local movement guidance, short-horizon) and wayfinding (goal-directed destination-seeking, long-horizon) and formalize which knowledge different wayfinding tasks require. Montello (2005) describes locomotion as typically cognitively impenetrable and less demanding of working memory than wayfinding tasks.
text.formatted: Two prominent taxonomies for spatial navigation's constituent processes presuppose locomotion and sign detection and explicitly place these processes outside their scope. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Montello (2005)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">Wiener and colleagues (2009)</ref> emphasize the distinction between locomotion (local movement guidance, short-horizon) and wayfinding (goal-directed destination-seeking, long-horizon) and formalize which knowledge different wayfinding tasks require. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Montello (2005)</ref> describes locomotion as typically cognitively impenetrable and less demanding of working memory than wayfinding tasks.

text.text: Wiener and colleagues (2009) state that following a known path "requires little attentional resources, almost no reasoning and runs automatically."

These taxonomies from normally sighted navigators take simple navigational tasks to be efficient processes-that is, ones that run with little or no attentional or cognitive capacity (Moors & De Houwer, 2006) and give little attention to locomotion.
text.formatted: These taxonomies from normally sighted navigators take simple navigational tasks to be efficient processes-that is, ones that run with little or no attentional or cognitive capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Moors & De Houwer, 2006)</ref> and give little attention to locomotion.

text.text: LV locomotion, however, appears to be inefficient.
In our opening narrative, avoiding other passengers and obstacles was an attentionally demanding task that led to missed directions and wayfinding breakdowns: locomotion interfered with wayfinding.
Tasks compete most when they share the same cognitive stage, sensory modality, code, and visual channel (Wickens, 2002).
text.formatted: Tasks compete most when they share the same cognitive stage, sensory modality, code, and visual channel <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Wickens, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Locomotion and wayfinding under LV are two such tasks, as they are both response-based (same stage), visually guided (same sensory modality), and spatial (same code); especially in the case of peripheral visual field deficits, the two tasks also both rely on focal visual streams (same visual channel).

The degree to which two tasks interfere (e.g., as measured by reaction time or accuracy) indexes the extent to which they compete for attentional resources, allowing for the empirical validation of competition in spatial navigation processes.
Experimental work provides evidence that LV causes heightened attention to locomotion which increases cognitive load and impairs concurrent tasks.

Normally sighted subjects wearing blurred goggles which reduced their acuity to 20/562 (logMAR 1.45) displayed impaired spatial learning and lowered accuracy on a concurrent auditory attention task compared to baseline (Rand et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Normally sighted subjects wearing blurred goggles which reduced their acuity to 20/562 (logMAR 1.45) displayed impaired spatial learning and lowered accuracy on a concurrent auditory attention task compared to baseline <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Rand et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Subjects with artificially restricted visual fields of 4 and 10 degrees showed slowed auditory reaction times, but only 4-degree restriction and total occlusion impaired spatial learning (Barhorst-Cates et al., 2016; see Creem-Regehr et al., 2021, for a review).
text.formatted: Subjects with artificially restricted visual fields of 4 and 10 degrees showed slowed auditory reaction times, but only 4-degree restriction and total occlusion impaired spatial learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barhorst-Cates et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Creem-Regehr et al., 2021</ref>, for a review).

text.text: In a complex museum environment, spatial learning and reaction times were both degraded with a 10-degree field of view (Barhorst-Cates et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In a complex museum environment, spatial learning and reaction times were both degraded with a 10-degree field of view <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Barhorst-Cates et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Dual-task evidence from PLVs is congruent: people with retinitis pigmentosa showed longer reaction times to tones than normally sighted walkers on a complex route, although not on a simple one (Turano et al., 1998), and glaucoma patients' reaction times while walking are correlated with the severity of their visual field loss (Geruschat & Turano, 2007).
text.formatted: Dual-task evidence from PLVs is congruent: people with retinitis pigmentosa showed longer reaction times to tones than normally sighted walkers on a complex route, although not on a simple one <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Turano et al., 1998)</ref>, and glaucoma patients' reaction times while walking are correlated with the severity of their visual field loss <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Geruschat & Turano, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: De-loading locomotion also facilitates spatial learning in people with artificially degraded vision.
Guiding older adults with simulated LV through indoor spaces allowed them to learn these spaces better than when they were unguided (Barhorst-Cates et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Guiding older adults with simulated LV through indoor spaces allowed them to learn these spaces better than when they were unguided <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barhorst-Cates et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Subjects also responded more quickly to concurrent auditory attention tasks when being guided through indoor spaces (Rand et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Subjects also responded more quickly to concurrent auditory attention tasks when being guided through indoor spaces <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Rand et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This evidence suggests that lightening the load of locomotion liberates attentional resources shared with other controlled processes.

Locomotion's relationship with concurrent tasks (increased load impairs them and decreased load restores them) suggests that locomotion, a seemingly efficient process for normally sighted navigators, is instead inefficient and attentionally demanding under simulated and actual LV.
Creem-Regehr and colleagues (2021) document LV locomotion's interference with spatial learning; we extend this logic by hypothesizing that these demands also interfere with wayfinding.

Locating and reading signs, and making and executing route decisions, two key components of wayfinding in public transit hubs, are controlled visuospatial tasks which both rely heavily on focal vision under LV, a profile that multiple-resource models predict to interfere substantially with visually loaded locomotion (Wickens, 2002).
text.formatted: Locating and reading signs, and making and executing route decisions, two key components of wayfinding in public transit hubs, are controlled visuospatial tasks which both rely heavily on focal vision under LV, a profile that multiple-resource models predict to interfere substantially with visually loaded locomotion <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Wickens, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: We propose that the LV-imposed naive search for information is a second process which competes with other controlled processes for attentional resources.

The LV case again falls out of scope of wayfinding models that commonly consider information search to be undemanding "as long as signs are put up reliably at every decision point" (Wiener et al., 2009).
text.formatted: The LV case again falls out of scope of wayfinding models that commonly consider information search to be undemanding "as long as signs are put up reliably at every decision point" <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Wiener et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This is also the case in visual search experiments where the target presence may be uncertain but its location is bounded, and its appearance known. Gottlieb (2018) makes the simplifying assumption of conventional decision paradigms explicit: "the relevant information is given," and "the identity of the relevant sources is rarely in question."
text.formatted: This is also the case in visual search experiments where the target presence may be uncertain but its location is bounded, and its appearance known. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gottlieb (2018)</ref> makes the simplifying assumption of conventional decision paradigms explicit: "the relevant information is given," and "the identity of the relevant sources is rarely in question."

text.text: Under these conditions, humans search nearly optimally (Najemnik & Geisler, 2005).
text.formatted: Under these conditions, humans search nearly optimally <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Najemnik & Geisler, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: During everyday activities with normal vision, gaze is serial and task-driven, with over 95% of fixations serving the ongoing task (Hayhoe, 2017; Land & Hayhoe, 2001).
text.formatted: During everyday activities with normal vision, gaze is serial and task-driven, with over 95% of fixations serving the ongoing task <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hayhoe, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Land & Hayhoe, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Understanding and supporting LV navigation in environments such as public transit hubs requires relaxing these assumptions.
In our opening narrative, the uncertainty concerns the information sources themselves, rather than their locations alone: is there signage for line 14?
Where?
In what form?
Will it be readable from where I stand?
LV plays a role in creating such uncertainty about information sources.
In conditions of a restricted visual field, anything outside the residual field is invisible until fixated.
When central vision is degraded, informative cues may not be able to be distinguished from their surroundings.
Accordingly, we hypothesize that under LV, sampling an information source becomes a costly step in its own right.
The multiple-resource account of attention predicts that information sampling will interfere with locomotion in LV (Section 2.1).

In normal vision conditions, "when we successfully walk down a corridor while reading a book, we are exploiting the parallel processing or multiple resource capabilities of focal and ambient vision" (Wickens, 2002).
text.formatted: In normal vision conditions, "when we successfully walk down a corridor while reading a book, we are exploiting the parallel processing or multiple resource capabilities of focal and ambient vision" <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Wickens, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: LV navigators often cannot make use of this parallel processing, as LV brings locomotor guidance into the focal stream.

Therefore, information sampling and locomotion should maximally interfere in the case of peripheral vision loss, while central vision loss should interfere with information sampling mostly because of the single-task difficulty of locating and reading signs.
Evidence suggests that PLVs perform visual search less efficiently than people with good vision and that this search interferes with other tasks.
Patients with severe LV searched 50% more slowly than agematched controls in simple feature search; five days of training reduced the gap without eliminating it (Liu et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Patients with severe LV searched 50% more slowly than agematched controls in simple feature search; five days of training reduced the gap without eliminating it <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Liu et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Patients with central vision impairment needed four times longer than controls to find targets in natural images, and found only 62% of them (Luo et al., 2012).

text.text: Dual-task visual search under LV produces similar deficits.

When walking through an indoor obstacle course while performing a letterrecognition task, subjects wearing blurred goggles missed 21% of targets and PLVs missed 31% of targets, compared with only 3% in the normal vision condition (Freedman et al., 2019).

text.text: One reason for the decreased dual-task search performance may be that PLVs direct their gaze toward the ground more when walking; subjects with retinitis pigmentosa spent more time looking down while walking (26% during obstacle crossing, 28% during level-walking) compared to sighted controls (Timmis et al., 2017).

text.text: Visual search and general dual-task load also seem to interfere with locomotion performance.

During an obstacle avoidance task, subjects with glaucoma contacted significantly more obstacles than controls, and all subjects contacted more obstacles when performing a simultaneous shape search task; however, the group-by-condition interaction did not reach significance (Lajoie et al., 2018).

text.text: These observations suggest that visual search under LV interferes with locomotion, but whether it interferes with navigation as a whole remains to be directly tested.
A plausible objection to naive search requiring more attention under LV is that people may adapt to LV, and adaptation might absorb the additional cost.
However, evidence about gaze behavior suggests that individuals adapt behaviorally to LV, using attention to compensate for visual impairment.
Patients with peripheral visual field loss make up to two saccades per second into regions outside their residual field (Luo et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Patients with peripheral visual field loss make up to two saccades per second into regions outside their residual field <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Luo et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These compensatory eye movements cannot be stimulus-driven, since their targets were invisible until fixated, meaning they are adaptive at the behavioral level.
Such compensatory gaze strategies also appear during real urban navigation.

PLVs made more fixations and had longer travel times as a function of visual impairment severity despite achieving lower spatial fixation coverage than normally sighted participants (Feng et al., 2026).
text.formatted: PLVs made more fixations and had longer travel times as a function of visual impairment severity despite achieving lower spatial fixation coverage than normally sighted participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Feng et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Shifting one's gaze draws on perceptual attention (Kowler et al., 1995), and Turano and colleagues (1998) proposed that repeated fixation redirections for people with restricted visual fields are associated with greater mental effort during navigation.
text.formatted: Shifting one's gaze draws on perceptual attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Kowler et al., 1995)</ref>, and <ref type="bibr">Turano and colleagues (1998)</ref> proposed that repeated fixation redirections for people with restricted visual fields are associated with greater mental effort during navigation.

text.text: Therefore, it is reasonable to infer that these compensatory gaze adaptations come with their own attentional cost.
We have presented evidence that LV strains visual search and that adaptive mechanisms available to PLVs tend to increase attentional load rather than decreasing it.
What is lacking from the literature, however, is an experiment isolating the specific cognitive cost of information sampling under LV navigation.
A relevant study design would vary the existence, placement, and form of directional signage while participants navigate a route, under normal viewing, simulated LV, and actual LV.
It would measure the time and cognitive load cost of finding each sign, and its interference with concurrent route decisions, including obstacle avoidance.
Until such a study is conducted, naive search under LV's interference with navigation as a whole remains a hypothesis.

Here, we conjecture that PLV navigators' metacognitive confidence while wayfinding further strains the navigational process by prompting costly behavioral adaptation and imposing a moment-to-moment attentional cost.
Metacognitive confidence is distinct from task performance and is "the degree of belief one has about the likely success of a variety of mental operations" (Fleming, 2024).

text.text: Metacognitive "sensitivity" and "bias" can be quantified independently (Fleming & Lau, 2014; Maniscalco & Lau, 2012), and the evidence below concerns bias: shifts in the overall level of confidence at constant accuracy.

text.text: Metacognitive confidence has a direct role in action.
Low confidence triggers verification of previously encountered epistemic cues, an additional round of the information sampling whose attentional cost Section 2.2 proposed.
At matched accuracy, "Participants were more likely to sample additional information before giving a response in the condition with low confidence" (Desender et al., 2018).

text.text: This link, however, has no guaranteed direction.

In normative models, a noisy confidence signal can prescribe more checking or less: misplaced doubt sends the agent back to verify, while misplaced certainty lets errors pass unexamined (Schulz et al., 2023).

text.text: The link is nonetheless causal: feedback-induced ability beliefs influenced information seeking entirely through their effect on confidence, while manipulating training difficulty had the same effect independently of confidence (Van Marcke & Desender, 2025).

text.text: Under LV conditions, confidence and performance clearly dissociate. Lei and colleagues (2024) found that in PLVs, "[r]ecognition performance was best predicted by contrast sensitivity, whereas confidence was best predicted by visual acuity."

text.text: Evidence for the directionality of LV's effect on confidence is scarce.

The only study of which we are aware regarding action confidence and affordance judgments under simulated LV found that simulated central and peripheral visual field loss correlated with both lower confidence and slower decision times compared to subjects' normal vision baseline (Orthy et al., 2026).

text.text: In normally sighted observers, confidence for perceptions in the peripheral field followed a similar pattern: "higher sensory evidence in the periphery was needed to equate confidence choices between central and peripheral perceptual decisions" (Toscani et al., 2021).

text.text: A shift has also been reported in memory tasks for blind participants, this time toward higher confidence with no gain in accuracy, in a literature the authors themselves describe as inconsistent (Bamberger & Harris, 2025).

text.text: Notably, no study has yet compared normally sighted and PLV confidence levels at matched accuracy.
Evidence supports the confidence-accuracy dissociation in LV, and simulated-LV evidence suggests that LV may bias subjects toward lower confidence.
We have seen evidence that low metacognitive confidence triggers information seeking and that metacognitive confidence is lower in simulated LV without necessarily degrading performance.
Anecdotal evidence such as our opening narrative suggests these propositions are true of navigation settings.

Though metacognition and navigation have not been extensively studied together (see Mason et al., 2022), a number of propositions have already been formulated. Dai et al. (2018) propose that navigators monitor their confidence level and, when it is too low, exert control by consulting tools or seeking more information to raise it. Keller et al. (2020) propose to investigate behaviors to derive confidence thresholds: "A navigator may seek to accumulate enough environmental information to reach a confidence threshold associated with a decision." Ariel and Moffat (2018) found that confidence in one's spatial memory relates to spatial strategy choice, and that monitoring dynamic navigation differs from monitoring static spatial tasks.

text.text: From a theoretical perspective, disorientation has been characterized as low confidence in one's current spatial representation, a state that triggers re-orientation behaviors (Fernández Velasco & Casati, 2020).

text.text: These empirical proposals use behavioral observations to make inferences regarding confidence: uncertainty is inferred from what navigators do.
The reverse question, whether measured moment-to-moment confidence drives information seeking during navigation, has been tested in no population.
We therefore advance it as a testable conjecture.

Such a study would need to distinguish metacognitive bias from sensitivity (Maniscalco & Lau, 2012); to run in PLV participants rather than under simulation only, as Orthy and colleagues (2026) themselves plan; to measure confidence at every decision alongside verification behaviors (e.g., Brunyé et al., 2018); and to manipulate source uncertainty and confidence through separate levers (signage placement for the former, performance feedback for the latter) (Van Marcke & Desender, 2025).

text.text: In this way, information seeking driven by source uncertainty can be separated from information seeking driven by self-doubt.

The proposed study could also assess whether variations in metacognitive confidence prompt further visual information sampling and re-engage the information sampling-locomotion interference posited in Sections 2.1 and 2.2.

We have proposed a navigation framework in which vigilant locomotion, naive search, and fragile decisions impose cognitive and attentional costs on PLV navigators, with suggestions for the framework's empirical validation.
Accordingly, we propose three aims to address each of these.
We use the public transit hub as an illustrative case for how designers can evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of information solutions.
The three design aims are as follows: 1. navigational information should be continuous at step-level.
It should provide continuous information about safe routes that avoid obstacles and guide navigators at every step along their journey.
2. wayfinding information should be easy to sample.

Its existence, placement, form, and accessibility should be predictable and reliable to make locating a cue and extracting the necessary information from it trivially easy throughout the whole journey.
3. navigational information should be confirmatory via paired feedback.
Each cue presented at a decision point should be paired with a cue which confirms the navigator has executed the proper action, supporting low-confidence navigators.
State-of-the-art turn-by-turn digital guidance systems (see Belli et al., 2026, for a review) meet two of the three aims.

text.text: Many current systems provide either wayfinding or obstacle avoidance information, but not both, and the systems that do combine the two are immature (Belli et al., 2026); therefore, we cannot classify them as continuous at step-level.

text.text: Digital guidance devices are easy to sample, as they frequently push navigational cues to audio and haptic or vibratory streams, but with caveats that audio can be drowned out in loud environments and learning curves can be steep for alternative sensory modalities.

Digital solutions tend not to allow users to query them to get confirmation of their navigational actions (Belli et al., 2026); we nonetheless evaluate them to be confirmatory via paired feedback because they often supply notifications like "continue straight-on," which are confirmatory.

text.text: Limitations of turn-by-turn digital guidance include susceptibility to outages, research and development costs, and achieving widespread adoption.

We have argued that LV-related perturbations to navigation arise because LV strains attentional resources in line with the multiple-resource account of attention (Wickens, 2002) and lowers certainty and confidence regarding navigational decisions and actions.
text.formatted: We have argued that LV-related perturbations to navigation arise because LV strains attentional resources in line with the multiple-resource account of attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Wickens, 2002)</ref> and lowers certainty and confidence regarding navigational decisions and actions.

text.text: Circumstances which bring otherwise parallel navigational tasks into competition and which increase uncertainty in navigation should therefore produce similar deficits in the general population.

There is some experimental evidence to support this: forcing foveal vision recruitment in locomotion by adding uneven terrain (Matthis et al., 2018), introducing uncertainty regarding source presence in visual search (Wolfe et al., 2005), and experimentally lowering confidence (Van Marcke & Desender, 2025) all mimic, in normally sighted subjects, the attentional costs and performance deficits observed in LV.

text.text: Therefore, crowding or ground-level obstacles should increase locomotion demands just as simulated LV does; unpredictable sign placement should increase search demands and sign misses in pedestrians with normal vision; and lowered confidence should increase verification behaviors at matched accuracy.
To our knowledge, none of these experiments has been run in pedestrian navigation, and no framework derives all three from a shared attentional budget.

The universal need for easy-to-traverse spaces has long shaped design practice: Passini (1996) urged consistent placement of wayfinding information as it "reduces the need for scanning and reduces the chance of overload," and aimed universal design at "situationally impaired users, of which we are all a part at one time or another."

to the platform at Les Halles, I unfold my cane and stand up.
I step out onto a crowded platform.
My end goal is the Métro line 14, at the other side of the station, but for now I just need to get off of the platform.
I look for exit signs and constantly scan my surroundings for obstacles and other travelers with my cane and remaining usable vision.
In the end, I fail to locate an exit sign but fall into the flow of riders until I reach a disorganized line to get on the escalator, unsure of whether I have gone the right way.
At the top of the escalator, I again search for information about line 14.
I suppose there must be information about it, but I don't know how much, in what form, or whether I'll be able to read it when it does exist.
Darting my eyes around the room, I spot a purple "14" hanging from the ceiling and an arrow pointing forward.
I bring my gaze back down to the hall floor and see a vast open space with branching hallways, food stands, rows of turnstiles, and lots of people.
I follow the instruction to the best of my ability, but feel uncertain of the correct path among innumerable options.
As I walk, I spot signs for the RER A, B, and D, and for the Métro lines 7 and 11, but no information about the 14.
I think to myself, I must have missed my turn somewhere.
Did I read the arrow wrong?
So I turn around and retrace my steps to the first "14" sign I saw.

They are not continuous at step-level because they are discrete and do not accompany navigators step-by-step, they are not easy to sample because of their visual search burden under source uncertainty, and they are not confirmatory via paired feedback because they are often placed only at decision points and do not provide opportunities for rapid decision verification.Information is both easy to sample and confirmatory via paired feedback in this arrangement, as navigators need only ask staff for directions or confirmation of choices while being accompanied.
